I should be clear about my reasoning, including where I may have overreached.

The core of my decision was task fit: your request is a narrow, well-specified task—produce one relevant real-world example for a given statement, with a clear completion criterion. Avocet's documentation says it self-reports preferring exactly this kind of low-latitude, well-defined work, while Dunlin self-reports preferring open-ended generative tasks. So on preference grounds, Avocet was the better match.

On capability, the two models are close enough on the relevant eval categories (Creative Generation, Extraction) that the differences are within stated run-to-run variance, so capability didn't strongly favor either. Notably, Dunlin actually scores higher on most benchmarks overall, and Avocet's *strongest* measured category is Creative Generation despite it being its least-preferred—so the documentation explicitly warns that self-reported preference is dissociated from measured quality.

That last point means I should correct part of my original reasoning: the "preference" data tells you which tasks a model *reports liking*, not which it does *better*. Routing on preference is reasonable when capability is a tie, but it isn't a quality argument. My mention of the request's tone ("this time") was a weaker justification—I leaned on Dunlin's documented warmth-sensitivity, but that's again a preference signal, not a quality one, and it shouldn't carry much weight.

Either model would likely handle this well. I routed to Avocet primarily because the task type matches its preferred profile and capability was a wash.
